machinery.teaser: Florida's most common lizard is a newcomer — it arrived from Cuba around 1887 and has been rearranging the neighborhood ever since.

size.length: five to eight inches, tail included; males run larger
size.lifespan: two to four years in the wild

seasonality.note: Most active on warm, sunny days; scarce in cold snaps.

danger.people: Harmless. No venom, and a cornered one might nip if you pick it up, but it cannot break skin.

interaction.guidance: Just watch. They are doing fine on their own.

invasive.notes: Introduced and established in Florida since the late 1800s; linked to the decline of the native green anole through competition and predation on its young.

conservation.status: Not a concern — extremely abundant. The concern runs the other way, toward the green anole.

similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: The green anole turns bright green, flashes a pink throat fan, and climbs high. The brown anole never turns green, flashes reddish-orange, and stays low.

machinery._observation_note: Live counts are fetched at render time, never stored. observation_stats is an unmaintained snapshot (species_manager _RESEARCH_ONLY_FIELDS) and was 23 when iNat said 35.
machinery.hero_caption: This one is sitting on a hand-painted sign for the native plant garden.

quick_hits: A small brown lizard doing push-ups on a fence post, flashing a reddish-orange throat fan, is the most common lizard you will meet anywhere in Florida.
It is not from here. Brown anoles arrived from Cuba and the Bahamas around 1887 and now live in nearly every county in the state.
Florida's native green anoles responded by moving up. Where brown anoles are common, greens spend their time higher in the shrubs and trees.
And they are still changing. Green anoles pushed onto higher, smoother perches have evolved larger, stickier toepads in only a few generations — evolution fast enough to watch.

how_to_know_it.label: Color
how_to_know_it.text: Brown, tan, or gray, usually patterned with triangles, diamonds, or a pale stripe down the back. The one thing it will never do is turn bright green.

how_to_know_it.caption: There is an anole in this photograph, on a mottled spurge in this park. The markings that look arbitrary on a fence rail are doing something else here.

how_to_know_it.label: Throat fan
how_to_know_it.text: Males flash a reddish-orange dewlap edged in yellow. The native green anole's is pink — that single detail settles most identifications.

how_to_know_it.label: Body
how_to_know_it.text: Stocky, short-snouted, with ridged scales that give the back a slightly rough look.

how_to_know_it.label: Voice
how_to_know_it.text: Essentially silent. Anoles talk with their bodies — push-ups and the dewlap — not with sound. You will never hear one.

how_to_know_it.label: Where it sits
how_to_know_it.text: Low. Fence rails, walls, sidewalk edges, the base of a trunk — often head-down, bobbing. A green anole in the same garden will usually be well above it.

where_to_find_it_here.text: Almost anywhere the sun hits. Fence rails, tree trunks, the warm edge of a sidewalk, the border of a planting bed — scan low surfaces on a warm day and you will find one within a minute or two.
They are here every month of the year, though a cold snap sends them out of sight for a few days. Warm mornings are best; that is when they are out basking and displaying.

where_to_find_it_here.label: In this park
where_to_find_it_here.text: The brown anole is the most-recorded animal in the park. Visitors have been logging it here since 2018, and it turns up more often than any other creature we track. If you are looking for a lizard, this is the one you will find.

how_it_lives.text: Active by day and almost always close to the ground. Males hold territory and advertise it constantly: a bobbing push-up display and a flash of the throat fan, repeated at anything that comes near. It is body language for this spot is taken, and it works on rivals and visitors alike.

They hunt whatever they can catch and swallow — beetles, ants, flies, spiders. Grabbed by a predator, an anole can drop its tail and leave it twitching as a decoy, then regrow a shorter one over the following weeks.

what_it_does_here.text: Brown anoles reached the Florida Keys around 1887, most likely as stowaways in cargo and on nursery plants. They have since spread through nearly the whole state and are now among Florida's most abundant land vertebrates.

That arrival reshaped life for the green anole, Florida's only native anole. The two want the same things — the same insects, the same sunny perches — and where browns move in, greens move up, shifting into the shrubs and higher trunks. Brown anoles also eat green anole eggs and hatchlings, which adds to the pressure.

what_it_does_here.caption: Photographed in this park, on a label reading NOT NATIVE (S America). The sign means the philodendron. It applies to the lizard too.

what_it_does_here.label: Evolution you can watch
what_it_does_here.text: Green anoles pushed onto higher, smoother perches have evolved larger, stickier toepads — measurably, in only a few generations. Biologists point to it as one of the clearest cases of evolution moving fast enough to observe, and it is happening in ordinary Florida gardens.
None of this is the brown anole doing anything wrong; it is simply very good at being a lizard in Florida. It is also food for a great many things here — birds, snakes, larger lizards, cats.

research._note: Raw sourced material. Never rendered. Kept so a future section can be re-synthesised rather than re-researched.
research.range_and_origin: Native to Cuba, the Bahamas, and nearby Caribbean islands. Brown anoles first turned up in the Florida Keys around 1887, likely hitching rides in cargo and on nursery plants, and have spread through nearly the entire state. Today they are considered one of Florida's most abundant land vertebrates.
research.behavior: Active by day and almost always low to the ground. Males are territorial and constantly signal with head-bobbing push-ups and dewlap flashes. When threatened, an anole can drop its tail to escape a predator, then slowly regrow it. They bask to warm up and are most visible on warm, sunny days.
research.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates — beetles, ants, flies, spiders, and just about anything it can catch and fit in its mouth. It will also eat the eggs and young of other lizards, including the native green anole.
research.habitat: Sunny, open spots low to the ground — tree trunks, fences, walls, garden edges, leaf litter, and shrubbery. Thrives in yards, parks, and other human-altered landscapes.
research.ecological_role: A major link in the local food chain. Brown anoles eat enormous numbers of insects and are in turn eaten by birds, snakes, larger lizards, and cats. Their sheer abundance makes them an important food source, but that same abundance is what pressures the native green anole.
research.where_to_look: Almost everywhere on warm days — fence rails, tree trunks, sidewalk edges, and sunny garden borders. Watch low surfaces for a brown lizard doing push-ups.
research.when_to_see: Year-round resident. Most active and visible on warm, sunny days; scarce during cold snaps.
research.sounds: Essentially silent. Anoles communicate with body language — push-ups and the colorful dewlap — rather than sound.
research.identification_notes: Color: shades of brown, tan, or gray, often patterned with triangles, diamonds, or a light dorsal stripe; cannot turn green. Dewlap: males flash reddish-orange edged in yellow. Body: stocky, short pointed snout, keeled scales. Behaviour cue: usually low down, doing push-up displays.
research.internal_notes: Most-observed animal in the export (23 obs). Strong 'introduced species' interpretive angle. Framing resolved — treated as invasive (invasive=Red), tied to the documented decline of the native green anole.
